author: sonnet
reason: A starts with how the current gateway works and why the counter has to live in a shared Redis. It also defines the project-specific terms an outsider lacks (Customer, Plan, Key Service), walks the flow in numbered steps tied to the diagram, and gathers every failure mode in one table, including Key Service outages and backend errors, which B never covers.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the better handoff for an outsider: it first explains the system as it stands today (6 stateless gateways, the Key Service, the 5-minute cache) and why Redis must be shared, defines the domain terms Customer, Plan and Key Service, and then ties numbered steps and a failure table to the diagram, while A starts with the new mechanism and leaves out the Key Service, backend-failure and cache-inconsistency cases.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to build a mental model from: it lays out three phases, then design decisions with their reasons, one guarded-copy rule and one reusable switch procedure (S) that it applies to the switch, the rollback and the finish, whereas A spreads the same mechanics across a long jargon-heavy terms list, a separate flow for each direction and step labels like "10d" that the terms list refers to before the steps are defined.

author: haiku
reason: B starts by explaining the existing system (scale, load, erasure job, StaleWrite, the unused pg-core pool), then walks through how writes, the relay, erasure, email conflicts and ids behave before and after the switch, with a failure table; A's tighter abstractions (guarded copy, procedure S) assume you already know the system.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a single mental model that runs in both directions (source of truth and follower, then commit, quick copy and repair through an outbox) and gives the reasons in a separate design-decisions section, so a newcomer understands how the system works before the checklist starts. A is thorough and precise, but it is dense with implementation detail from the start, such as SQL in the term definitions and per-path edge cases, and that makes the overall shape harder to see.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I'd want to be handed. It starts with the current state, then explains how writes, deletes, reads and the switch work in their own section, apart from the rollout steps, and ends with a failure table. A opens with a clearer short summary, but it spreads the important details (drainer behaviour, the dual-write path, read freshness) across individual checklist steps.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how double-charge prevention actually works: claim rows with a unique constraint and specific states, per-charge steps, a drain, and handoff of released claims. It also lists failures in a table and keeps assumptions separate. B reads more easily but stays vague on the mechanism (a check-then-charge ledger lookup and an undefined "fence") and contradicts itself, saying rollback ends in old_only and also that the rollout returns to shadow.

author: haiku
reason: Document A explains the whole rollout quickly and clearly: the four modes, the fence-settle-reconcile-flip rollback order, where state lives and what happens on failure. Document B is more rigorous about the claim mechanism, but its length, long state names and many open questions and assumptions make the core model harder to pick up for someone new to the system.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for an outsider to follow because it does three things A doesn't. It states the two governing rules first. Its diagram labels every state with plain meanings and shows retries as self-loops. And it spells out the mechanisms concretely: the four reconcile outcomes, plus the idempotency key and the ledger uniqueness constraint that block double charges. A is precise but denser, and a dozen caveats and open questions get in the way of the main flow.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow: it defines its terms first, then gives a flat diagram, a mode table that splits new_only by day, rollback steps in one fixed order, and plain charge-safety rules (idempotency key plus a ledger uniqueness constraint), while Document B covers more edge cases but is denser, piles on twelve open questions, and admits its own reprocess step may not be needed, which blurs the overall picture.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with an overview that explains why the flow is ordered as it is, then covers the mechanics an outsider would otherwise have to guess: the browser's async polling, the outbox relay, crash recovery, polling for a missing webhook, the expiry and claim race, and idempotency at each step. B reads more easily but leaves crash and lost-message behaviour unexplained.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer than A, but it opens with a summary of the saga and the reasons behind it (reserve stock before charging, claim only after payment succeeds), then answers what an engineer asks next and A leaves open: crash recovery, at-least-once delivery, double-clicks, lost responses and charges that never resolve.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with the whole flow and explains why the steps come in this order (the 10-minute hold against a webhook that can take up to 30 minutes), and it spells out the edge cases B leaves out: calls that get no answer, a success that arrives for an order that already failed, a silent provider, and the outbox relay going down, so a newcomer gets a complete and consistent model even though its flowchart is denser than B's.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a one-sentence summary and a reading guide, then defines its terms and keeps a clean flowchart with the failure paths marked, so a newcomer can grasp the system quickly; B covers more edge cases (timeouts, CHECKOUT_FAILED, a silent provider, the relay being down), but its crowded chart, inconsistent arrow legend and nested exceptions make it harder to learn from first.
